questions.answer: An antiderivative differentiates back to the integrand. Since \(\frac{d}{dx}(7x)=7\), one antiderivative is \(7x\). The full indefinite integral is \(7x+C\).

questions.prompt: What term must be included in \(\int f(x)\,dx\) to represent all antiderivatives?
questions.answer: Include the constant of integration, \(C\). If \(F'(x)=f(x)\), then \((F(x)+C)'=f(x)\) for every constant \(C\).

questions.prompt: Complete the statement: if \(F'(x)=f(x)\), then \(\int f(x)\,dx=\,?\)
questions.answer:
The indefinite integral is the family of antiderivatives:
\[\int f(x)\,dx=F(x)+C.\]
Differentiating any constant gives zero. Therefore \(x^3\), \(x^3+5\), and \(x^3-12\) all differentiate to \(3x^2\). The \(+C\) records all such possibilities.

Use the power rule with \(n=4\):
\[\int x^4\,dx=\frac{x^{5}}{5}+C.\]

Integrate the power and keep the constant factor:
\[\int 6x^2\,dx=6\cdot\frac{x^3}{3}+C=2x^3+C.\]

Integrate term by term:
\[\int4x^3\,dx=x^4,\quad \int(-5)\,dx=-5x.\]
Therefore
\[\int(4x^3-5)\,dx=x^4-5x+C.\]

Integrate each term:
\[\int3x^2\,dx=x^3,\quad \int(-4x)\,dx=-2x^2,\quad \int8\,dx=8x.\]
So
\[\int(3x^2-4x+8)\,dx=x^3-2x^2+8x+C.\]

Write \(\sqrt{x}=x^{1/2}\).
\[\int2x^{1/2}\,dx=2\cdot\frac{x^{3/2}}{3/2}=\frac{4}{3}x^{3/2}.\]
Also \(\int 3/x\,dx=3\ln x\) because \(x>0\).
Thus the answer is \(\frac{4}{3}x^{3/2}+3\ln x+C\).

First integrate:
\[F(x)=x^5-x^2+C.\]
Use \(F(1)=10\):
\[1-1+C=10\Rightarrow C=10.\]
Therefore \(F(x)=x^5-x^2+10\).

questions.prompt: Verify that \(F(x)=\frac{x^5}{5}-3x+C\) is an antiderivative of \(x^4-3\).
questions.answer:
Differentiate \(F\):
\[F'(x)=\frac{1}{5}\cdot5x^4-3+0=x^4-3.\]
Since the derivative equals the integrand, \(F(x)\) is an antiderivative of \(x^4-3\).

Rewrite \(2/\sqrt{x}=2x^{-1/2}\).
\[\int2x^{-1/2}\,dx=2\cdot\frac{x^{1/2}}{1/2}=4\sqrt{x}.\]
Also
\[\int(-x^{-2})\,dx=-\frac{x^{-1}}{-1}=x^{-1}.\]
So the integral is \(4\sqrt{x}+\frac1x+C\).

Differentiate the proposed antiderivative:
\[\frac{d}{dx}(2x^3+4x+C)=6x^2+4.\]
This must equal \(ax^2+4\), so \(a=6\).

questions.prompt: For which \(n\) does the power rule formula \(\int x^n\,dx=\frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}+C\) fail, and what integral replaces it?
questions.answer:
The formula fails when \(n+1=0\), so \(n=-1\), because division by zero would occur. In that case
\[\int x^{-1}\,dx=\int\frac1x\,dx=\ln|x|+C.\]

Integrate first:
\[F(x)=x^2+kx+C.\]
Use \(F(0)=3\), giving \(C=3\). Use \(F(2)=15\):
\[4+2k+3=15\Rightarrow 2k=8\Rightarrow k=4.\]
Thus \(F(x)=x^2+4x+3\).

questions.prompt: A student writes \(\int x^{-1}\,dx=\frac{x^0}{0}+C\). Explain the error and give the correct antiderivative.
questions.answer:
The power rule \(x^{n+1}/(n+1)\) requires \(n\ne-1\). For \(n=-1\), the denominator is zero, so the rule is not valid. The correct result is
\[\int x^{-1}\,dx=\ln|x|+C.\]

questions.prompt: Show that any two antiderivatives of the same function differ by a constant, assuming the fact that a function with derivative zero on an interval is constant.
questions.answer:
Let \(F'(x)=f(x)\) and \(G'(x)=f(x)\) on the same interval. Then
\[(F-G)'=F'-G'=f(x)-f(x)=0.\]
By the stated fact, \(F-G\) is constant. Therefore \(F(x)=G(x)+C\), so any two antiderivatives differ only by a constant.

questions.prompt: Find all functions \(F\) such that \(F'(x)=6x^2-4x+1\) and \(F(1)-F(0)=5\), or explain if none exist.
questions.answer:
Integrate:
\[F(x)=2x^3-2x^2+x+C.\]
Then
\[F(1)-F(0)=(2-2+1+C)-C=1.\]
The difference is forced to be \(1\), regardless of \(C\). Since the required difference is \(5\), no such function exists.
